title: When Team Members and Performers Reach a Plateau and Stop Developing
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses the common phenomenon of performers hitting a plateau where prior strengths stop producing further gains — what psychologists call 'arrested development.' The author lays out five specific levers for breaking through: setting new (and more uncomfortable) goals, changing training and practice methods, shifting focus toward correcting weaknesses rather than amplifying strengths, bringing in a new coach or feedback source, and changing the timing of self-reflection relative to performance. A recurring theme is discomfort as a signal of real growth — if practice feels easy or enjoyable, it's probably not challenging enough to produce new learning. The piece closes with a memorable line comparing plateaus to quicksand.
points: Performance plateaus ('arrested development') happen to nearly everyone, and continuing to do what previously worked guarantees the stall continues.

Breaking a plateau requires deliberately changing one of five levers: new goals, new training methods, a shift toward addressing weaknesses instead of amplifying strengths, a new coach or feedback source, or a new timing for reflection.
Research suggests that during stagnation, focusing on weaknesses yields more progress than the usual strategy of amplifying strengths.
Comfortable, routine practice is a red flag during a plateau — if practice isn't difficult, it likely isn't producing new learning.
quotes: Psychologists call this stall in improvement “arrested development,” and it happens to just about everyone at some point.
As long as team members and performers continue to do what has taken them this far, they are doomed to flatline in their progress.
In fact, if practice is enjoyable, it probably isn’t hard enough.
Research on performers who reach a performance plateau shows that top performers can break free by fixating more on their biggest weaknesses.
Plateaus are okay to visit, but no one wants to live there. Top performers and team members will do what it takes to reach the next level of mastery. Anything else is quicksand.
